Here are the verse-by-verse notes compiled from the sources I was able to access.

---

## 1 Kings 8:23–44 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview of the Prayer (vv. 23–53)

Ellicott describes Solomon's prayer as "of extreme simplicity of idea." It begins (a) with thankful acknowledgment of the fulfillment of one part of the Davidic promise and prayer for the other (vv. 23–25); (b) then acknowledges that God's presence cannot be limited to any temple, yet asks that His blessing rest on prayer made toward that hallowed place (vv. 26–30); (c) then applies that petition to seven specific contingencies: oaths, defeat, drought, famine/pestilence, the foreigner, war, and captivity (vv. 31–53). The "constantly recurring burden" is: "Hear Thou from heaven thy dwelling-place, and when Thou hearest, Lord, forgive." Ellicott notes that before Solomon's mind the blessings and curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 are continually present.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

---

### v. 23 – "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven above or on earth below, keeping Your covenant of loving devotion with Your servants who walk before You with all their hearts."

**Traditional reading:**
Solomon begins his prayer with praise. The Pulpit Commentary observes that Solomon "begins his prayer with an act of praise; with a recognition at once grateful and graceful of God's past mercies." It adds that similar words are found in Exodus 15:11 and Psalm 86:8 and that they "do not at all imply the existence of other gods," but are explained by other passages (Deut 4:39; 2 Sam 7:22) as meaning that the God of Israel "stands alone, and alone is God."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html

Gill explains: "their covenant God and Father, whereby he was distinguished from all the gods of the Gentiles… none among the angels in heaven, nor among kings and civil magistrates on earth, who both are sometimes called 'Elohim' gods; but only in a figurative sense, and not to be compared with the one only true God."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/8.htm

Ellicott traces the phrase "there is no God like Thee" from the Song at the Red Sea (Ex 15:11), through David's thanksgiving (2 Sam 7:22), to Solomon. He notes a spiritual progression: from the God "to whom none is like" among the gods others worshipped, to the "God Almighty, Judge of the whole earth," to Jehovah the One Self-existent Being.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

David Guzik (Enduring Word, Pentecostal/charismatic tradition) notes that Solomon recognized God as "completely unique. The pretended gods of the other nations could not compare to Him in any way."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 24 – "You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David. What You spoke with Your mouth You have fulfilled with Your hand this day."

The Pulpit Commentary notes that Solomon sees in the completed temple "a special pledge of God's faithfulness and truth." The completion of the house, together with Solomon's establishment on the throne, was to him "proof conclusive that the promise of 2 Samuel 7 had received its fulfilment." The Hebrew plays on the word "spakest" — "thou spakest also with thy mouth and hast fulfilled it with thine hand."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html

Guzik says Solomon "first thanked and praised God for His past fulfillment of promises."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 25 – "Therefore now, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant, my father David, what You promised when You said: 'You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your descendants guard their way to walk before Me as you have done.'"

The Pulpit Commentary observes that "the promise has been but partially fulfilled. The house is built; he now prays that the succession may be continued in David's line." The commentary also notes the play on the word "keep": God's keeping His promise was contingent on David's descendants keeping His commandments. The condition "so that" (marg. "if only") is key: "God's keeping His promise was contingent on their keeping His commandments."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html

Ellicott adds an important qualification: the larger part of the Davidic promise (2 Sam 7:12–16; Ps 89:28–37) expressly declares that even if David's seed fall away, "they shall indeed be chastised, but they shall not be cast off." The actual enjoyment of blessing by each generation is conditional, but the promise itself is fixed and immutable, compared to "the ordinances of the sun and moon" (Jer 31:36; 33:20–26).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) says: "Solomon called upon God to keep the promises that He made. This is the great secret to power in prayer – to take God's promises to heart in faith, and then to boldly and reverently call upon Him to fulfill the promises." He quotes Spurgeon: "God sent the promise on purpose to be used… nothing pleases God better than to see his promises put in circulation."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 26 – "And now, O God of Israel, please confirm what You promised to Your servant, my father David."

Guzik notes: "This kind of prayer lays hold of God's promise. Just because God promises does not mean that we possess. Through believing prayer like this, God promises and we appropriate. If we don't appropriate in faith, God's promise is left unclaimed."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 27 – "But will God indeed dwell upon the earth? Even heaven, the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this temple I have built."

This is one of the great theological statements of the Old Testament. Ellicott explains: "The thought expressed here exemplifies a constant antithesis which runs through the Old Testament. On the one hand, there is the most profound and unvarying conception of the Infinity, eternal, invisible, incomprehensible, of the Lord… and the spirituality of this conception is guarded by the sternest prohibition of that idolatry which limited and degraded the idea of God… On the other hand, there is an equally vivid conviction that the Infinite Jehovah is yet pleased to enter into a special covenant with Israel." The Temple is "the place where God's 'Name' — that is, His self-revelation — is made to dwell; but heaven, and it alone, as the true dwelling-place of God Himself." Ellicott adds that Solomon's words "in spirit anticipate the utterance of the prophet (Isaiah 66:1), quoted by St. Stephen against idolatry of the Temple (Acts 7:48), and even the greater declaration of our Lord (John 4:21-24) as to the universal presence of God to all spiritual worship."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

Dr. Constable's Expository Notes (evangelical) comment: "Solomon voiced the truth that Yahweh did not really live on earth but in heaven. He did not confuse the symbols of God's presence with God Himself (cf. 1 Sam 4:3)."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-8.html

Guzik: "We are glad that Solomon said this. From his statement in 1 Kings 8:12-13, we might have thought that he drifted towards a superstitious idea that God actually lived in the temple to the exclusion of other places."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 28 – "Yet regard the prayer and plea of Your servant, O LORD my God, so that You may hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You today."

Solomon, having acknowledged God's transcendence, now asks Him to "regard" (turn toward) his prayer anyway. Guzik observes the humility: God is infinitely great, yet Solomon asks Him to incline His ear.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 29 – "May Your eyes be open toward this temple night and day, toward the place of which You said, 'My Name shall be there,' so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place."

The key phrase is "My Name shall be there." Ellicott notes the instructive contrast: the Temple is where God's Name (His self-revelation) dwells; heaven alone is where God Himself dwells.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

Guzik notes that "for this reason, many observant Jews still pray facing the direction of the site of the temple in Jerusalem."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### v. 30 – "Hear the plea of Your servant and of Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. May You hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. May You hear and forgive."

Guzik: "Solomon knew that the most important thing Israel needed was forgiveness. This was the greatest answer to prayer Israel could expect from God."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary: "Under one word, 'forgive,' Solomon expressed all that he could ask in behalf of his people. For, as all misery springs from sin, forgiveness of sin prepares the way for the removal of every evil, and the receiving of every good. Without it, no deliverance can prove a blessing."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/1-kings-8.html

---

### vv. 31–32 – The Oath Case: "When a man sins against his neighbor and is required to take an oath, and he comes to take an oath before Your altar in this temple, then may You hear from heaven and act. May You judge Your servants, condemning the wicked man by bringing down on his own head what he has done, and justifying the righteous man by rewarding him according to his righteousness."

Guzik explains: "The temple grounds were used as a place to verify and authorize oaths. When a dispute came down to one word against another, Solomon asked that the temple would be a place to properly swear by." He adds that Solomon asked "the God who can see what man can't – who knows the hidden heart of man – to enforce from heaven the oaths made at the temple." Guzik also relays a colorful note from the Puritan John Trapp about a woman in 1575 London who swore falsely and "fell down presently speechless, and with horrible stink died."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

The Pulpit Commentary Homiletics notes that this is the first of seven specific cases where Solomon asks God to "hear from heaven."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html

---

### vv. 33–34 – Defeat in Battle: "When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they return to You and confess Your name, praying and pleading with You in this temple, then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel. May You restore them to the land You gave to their fathers."

Guzik: "Many times in their history, Israel suffered defeat and could only cry out to God. It was even worse when the defeat was because they had sinned against the LORD Himself." He emphasizes the condition: "when they turn back to You and confess Your name… God answered this prayer of Solomon, and He forgives and restores His defeated people when they come in humble repentance."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

Dr. Constable notes that all the calamities Solomon mentions are curses God promised to send on Israel if she broke the Mosaic Covenant (cf. Lev 26:16–39; Deut 28:22, 25, 38, 42, 59).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-8.html

---

### vv. 35–36 – Drought: "When the skies are shut and there is no rain because Your people have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your name, and they turn from their sins because You have afflicted them, then may You hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants… May You send rain on the land…"

Guzik notes that "drought was a constant threat for the agriculturally-based economy of Israel. If there was no rain, there was no food." He also emphasizes grace: "Solomon doesn't take it for granted that God would forgive and hear His repentant people. God's good response to our repentance comes from His grace, not from justice."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

Ellicott says: "Solomon dwells on the plague of famine, from rain withheld, by which, in the striking language of the Law, 'the heaven is shut up'" (Deut 11:17). The affliction is designed to drive the people to repentance.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

---

### vv. 37–40 – Famine, Plague, and Every Affliction: "When famine or plague comes upon the land, or blight or mildew or locusts or grasshoppers, or when their enemy besieges them in their cities, whatever plague or sickness may come, then may whatever prayer or petition Your people Israel make—each knowing his own afflictions and spreading out his hands toward this temple—be heard by You from heaven… repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart—for You alone know the hearts of all men—so that they may fear You all the days they live in the land…"

**"Each knowing his own afflictions" (v. 38) / "the plague of his own heart":**

Ellicott explains that Solomon passes on to the various plagues threatened in the Law — famine, pestilence, blasting, mildew, locust, caterpillar (Lev 26:25–26; Deut 28:22–24, 38–42), the distress of siege (Deut 28:52–57) — and then sums up with "whatsoever plague, whatsoever sickness." Through any or all of these, "he pictures each man as brought to 'know the plague of his own heart' — that is, as startled into a consciousness of sin, and recognition of it as the true 'plague,' the cause of all outward plagues, and so drawn to prayer of penitence and of godly fear."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

Guzik: "Solomon recognized that some plagues are easily seen, but other plagues come from our own heart. Many are cursed by a plague that no one else can see, but lives in their own heart." He quotes Spurgeon: "A great many men think they know the plague of other people's hearts… I pray you let the scandals of the hour alone, and think of your own evils."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

Matthew Henry: "Sin is the plague of our own hearts; our in-dwelling corruptions are our spiritual diseases: every true Israelite endeavours to know these, that he may mortify them, and watch against the risings of them. These drive him to his knees; lamenting these, he spreads forth his hands in prayer."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhn/1-kings-8.html

**"You alone know the hearts of all men" (v. 39):**

Guzik notes that "a man did not have to be sinless or righteous to have his prayer answered at the temple. He could be a guilty man, stricken by the plague of his own heart, and still find a gracious God when He came in humble repentance."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

---

### vv. 41–43 – The Foreigner: "And as for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land because of Your name—for they will hear of Your great name and mighty hand and outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this temple, then may You hear from heaven… and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to You. Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as do Your people Israel, and they will know that this house I have built is called by Your Name."

**Traditional reading:**

Guzik emphasizes the missionary impulse: "The temple was in Israel, but it was always intended to be a house of prayer for all nations (Isaiah 56:7). God wanted the court of the Gentiles to be a place where the nations could come and pray." He notes that "the violation of this principle made Jesus angry. When He came to the temple and found the outer courts… more like a swap meet than a house of prayer, He drove out the moneychangers and the merchants (Matthew 21:13)." Guzik adds: "Solomon asked God to hear the prayer of the foreigner out of a missionary impulse. He knew that when God mercifully answered the prayers of foreigners, it drew those from other nations to the God of all nations."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-8/

Ellicott notes the breadth of Solomon's vision: the prayer extends God's hearing "not only to Israel, but to the stranger who shall acknowledge and invoke the Lord Jehovah."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-8.html

**Application across traditions:**

This passage is prized in evangelical missions theology as an Old Testament warrant for the inclusion of Gentiles. While I could not fetch separate denominational treatments within my limits, the consistent note across Guzik (Pentecostal), Constable (evangelical), Ellicott (Anglican), and the Pulpit Commentary (broad Protestant) is that this is a striking early expression of God's heart for the nations.

---

### v. 44 – "When Your people go to war against their enemies, wherever You send them, and when they pray to the LORD in the direction of the city You have chosen and the house I have built for Your Name…"

The Pulpit Commentary observes that the wording "whithersoever thou shalt send them" clearly implies that the war "is one which had God's sanction, and indeed was waged by His appointment." It adds a play on the Hebrew phrasing: "They have gone in God's way. They may therefore look the way of God's house for help. Executing God's commission, they might justly expect His blessing."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-8.html

Gill notes the same point: "notwithstanding the justness of their cause, and having a warrant from God to go to war, yet they were to pray to him for success when at a distance, even in a foreign land, and about to engage the enemy; and this they were to do, turning their faces towards the city of Jerusalem, and the temple there; declaring thereby that their dependence was upon the Lord that dwelt there."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/8.htm

Dr. Constable includes this as the sixth of Solomon's seven petitions, noting that prayer toward the temple and Jerusalem demonstrated dependence on God even when the people were far from the land.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-8.html

---

## Summary of Key Themes Across Traditions

1. **God's uniqueness and covenant faithfulness** (v. 23): All commentators agree Solomon begins with praise and acknowledges God as incomparable.

2. **Prayer that lays hold of promise** (vv. 24–26): Guzik (Pentecostal) and Spurgeon (Baptist/reformed) particularly emphasize "appropriating" God's promises through bold, believing prayer — a theme often associated with charismatic and Baptist piety. Ellicott carefully balances this with the unconditional aspect of the Davidic covenant.

3. **God's transcendence and immanence** (vv. 27–30): All traditions see this as a profound theological statement. Ellicott connects it to the New Testament (Acts 7:48; John 4:21–24). The Temple houses God's "Name," but heaven is His dwelling.

4. **Repentance as the key to restoration** (vv. 33–40): Every calamity is tied to sin and the remedy is always repentance, confession, and turning toward God. This reflects the theology of Deuteronomy and the Mosaic covenant blessings and curses.

5. **The foreigner and the nations** (vv. 41–43): Universally seen as a missionary text. The temple was always meant to be "a house of prayer for all nations."

6. **Prayer directed toward the temple** (v. 44): The physical orientation toward Jerusalem and the temple expressed spiritual dependence on the God who dwelt there by His Name.

---

*Note: I was unable within available searches and fetches to locate distinct treatments from Catholic (newadvent.org/catholic.com), Orthodox (oca.org), Lutheran (lcms.org/1517.org), or modern scholarly sources (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org) for this specific passage, nor any "prosperity gospel" or "word of faith" readings. The denominational differences that do emerge above are modest: Ellicott (Anglican) emphasizes the Christological and covenant-theological arc toward the New Testament; Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) emphasizes the boldness of appropriating God's promises in prayer; the Reformed tradition (via Spurgeon as quoted) similarly emphasizes pleading God's promises, though from a doctrine-of-grace framework.*
